body:
There are two parts of this problem. 

**misconfiguration**
The root cause of the error is that the project is misconfigured. The TypeScript compiler is unable to resolve `@service-work/is-loading`. This can be resolved by setting as path mappings in your tsconfig.

```js
{
  "compileOnSave": false,
  "compilerOptions": {
    ...
    "paths": {
      "@service-work/is-loading": ["projects/is-loading/build"]
    }
  }
}
``` 


**compiler-cli**

The compiler-cli is surfacing this particular error as a `FatalDiagnosticError`, which should not happen and therefore this is also an issue in the compiler-cli, which should converted this to a `ts.Diagnostic` internally.

body:
I was having a similar issue when trying to build my shared-components library when also using an Angular workspace to hold a few Angular apps. Unlike the `@service-work/is-loading` and `@service-work/scroll-position`  packages, I wanted my library to only be used locally. 

I'm also using Angular 13.2.

```
my-workspace git:(template) ✗ ng build shared-components
Building Angular Package

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Building entry point 'shared-components'
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
✖ Compiling with Angular sources in Ivy partial compilation mode.
Schema validation failed with the following errors:
  Data path "/error" must be string.
```

The error was caused by two things (that I think only happened because I was using a workspace):
1. `public-api.ts` file was contained within a `projects` folder that lived adjacently to the `lib` folder and inside `src`
2. The export statements in the `public-api.ts` file were incorrect, giving the error `Cannot find module... or its corresponding type declarations` error

Moving the file outside the folder, correcting the exports, and renaming the `entryFile` field in the ng-package.json solved the issue. For me, no other changes to ts.config.json files were needed.

To use my library, I first built it using `ng build shared-components --watch` and then imported into my module like this:

```ts
import { SharedComponentsModule } from 'shared-components'
// other imports...

const COMPONENTS = [ /* components to use across app */ ]
const ANGULAR_MODULES = [CommonModule, RouterModule]

const MODULES = [
  ...ANGULAR_MODULES,
  SharedComponentsModule,
  // other modules...
]

@NgModule({
  declarations: [...COMPONENTS],
  // declarations: [...COMPONENTS, ...PIPES],
  exports: [...COMPONENTS, ...MODULES],
  providers: [],
  imports: [...MODULES],
})
export class ComponentsModule {}
```

Then I can use any component, service, etc. in any place in my app!

I'm not sure why Angular would generate the public-api.ts file inside a folder when using workspaces. I'd hoped to have it work out the box, but it cost me an hour or two of problem solving.

@PhiLhoSoft, you can add a console log or breakpoint here: https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/blob/e1d9b5b447b67c028e84fd764e4ae390300f92a7/packages/angular_devkit/build_angular/src/builders/ng-packagr/index.ts#L61

body:
Update: I had this error after adding a component to the library project.
I had another look at the component, and finally spotted the culprits: I routinely import classes by typing their name, then hitting Enter on the suggestion made by VSC.
But I didn't see it made `import { SomeClass } from 'api';` where there is no definition of this `api` thing.
It should have been `import { SomeClass } from 'the-current-project/api';` because in `tsconfig.json`, I defined in the `paths` section: `'the-current-project/*': ['./*'],`
And then, it worked…

Note 1: the `'Unable to import symbol AddressbookAvatarComponent.'` message is totally unrelated to the new component which doesn't use this one. This is why it was hard to track…
Note 2: beware, sometime VSC also makes `import { Foo ] from '../';` (or `from './';`) because there is an `index.ts` file at this location (it is used to export models, services, modules, components, etc. Barrel files.). These imports creates subtle bugs too, perhaps cyclic dependencies. Change them to `import { Foo ] from '../foo.ts';` for example.

issue.body:
An inline type-check block is required when a reference to a component class
cannot be emitted from an ngtypecheck shim file, but the logic to detect this
situation did not consider the configured `rootDir`. When a `rootDir` is
configured the reference emitter does not allow generating an import outside
this directory, which meant that a shim file wouldn't be able to reference
the component class. Consequently, type-check block generation would fail
with a fatal error that is unaccounted for, as gathering diagnostics should
be non-fallible.

This commit fixes the problem by leveraging the existing `canReferenceType`
logic of the type-checking `Environment`, instead of the rudimentary check
whether the class is exported as top-level symbol (`checkIfClassIsExported`).
Instead, `canReferenceType` pre-flights the generation of an import using the
`ReferenceEmitter` to tell exactly whether it will succeed or not; thus taking
into account the `rootDirs` constraint as well.

Fixes #44999
